title: Video deepfakes and business email compromise
body_md:
## Familiar faces, a changed account

Picture a video grid of familiar faces, the finance director's among them, and a chat message saying a supplier's bank account changed this morning. Everyone looks calm. Nobody has checked the one thing that matters.

Business email compromise (BEC) aims to redirect a transfer, or to change the account behind a real invoice. The attacker may control a lookalike address, a hijacked mailbox, a chat account or a meeting invitation. Video adds the look of proof, but the decision turns on a different question: **who authorised this exact payment to this exact beneficiary?**

### One documented case

In January 2024, according to the account the Hong Kong Government gave in June that year, a worker received a phishing email that claimed to come from the CFO of the company's UK head office. The worker then watched a **pre-recorded, fabricated group conference**, authorised transfers to five local accounts and received further instructions by instant message. The reported loss was about HK$200 million, and the case was still under investigation when the official reply was given. It is a documented example of a recording standing in for a meeting, not evidence that the impostors held a live discussion. The exercises below are invented.

An attacker can choose the meeting platform and line up familiar faces and voices. Odd video can also have a dull cause: compression, a virtual background, poor lighting. Asking someone to turn their head may raise a concern, but it clears no payment either way. A convincing recording can show no seams, and a real colleague can freeze on screen. A call tells you about a request. It is not the control that releases money.

### What actually releases the money

For a payment or a change of beneficiary, compare the new instructions with the existing vendor record. Call a number from records created before the request arrived. Get the separate approval your procedure requires, and write down what you verified. A message from a genuine internal account is not always enough, because the account itself may be compromised. If a manager cannot be reached, hold the change and escalate by the documented route; confidentiality is never a reason to skip it. If a transfer has already gone out, call the bank at once and ask about a recall. Recovery is not certain.

**In practice:** use the same control for an ordinary call, a video call and a polished email. The impersonation technique will keep changing; the check on the beneficiary and the chain of authority should not.

widget_config.goal: Apply payment-change controls even when the request arrives in a convincing video meeting.
widget_config.today_action: Find your organisation’s rule for approving a new beneficiary, and name the independent contact you would call back.
widget_config.scope: Workplace education. The Hong Kong example is a dated official account from 2024, and the US IC3 advice applies to the US. Follow your own employer’s and bank’s procedures. The cases and the exercise below are invented.

sources.title: Hong Kong Government: Legislative Council reply on deepfake fraud
sources.scope: Dated 26 June 2024. Reports a January case with a pre-recorded, fabricated conference and later instructions by messaging. The investigation was still under way at that date, and the case is not an example of a live interactive call.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Business Email Compromise
sources.scope: US guidance on transfer and account-change requests: verify through a second channel, and contact the bank urgently after a suspected transfer. Organisational and national procedures vary.

blocks.title: The “CFO” on camera, a new account in the chat
blocks.situation: A video meeting shows the CFO and two colleagues. In the chat, a message says a supplier’s bank account changed this morning and the transfer has to go out now.
blocks.analysis: Several faces and a chat message add up to one source, not two approvals. Hold the change, call the supplier and the CFO on numbers from existing records, and complete the separate sign-off. The video could be generated, recorded, or real and sitting on a compromised account; the control is the same.

blocks.title: A real vendor, a bad connection
blocks.situation: On a routine video call, a vendor you know freezes, and the picture drifts out of step with their voice. The invoice on the table and the destination account are unchanged.
blocks.analysis: Weak connections and heavy compression do this all the time. Do not call the vendor a fraudster on the evidence of pixels. If the conversation matters, reconnect through the usual meeting route, and carry on with the normal invoice checks.

blocks.title: The acquisition meeting
blocks.setup: An invented scenario: the finance team of a company in the middle of an acquisition is invited to an urgent video meeting about a changed escrow recipient. Each decision is a fresh start; what you did in one does not carry into the next.

steps.prompt: A familiar face says the deal is confidential. What do you write down?

choices.consequence: The account the money would go to is still unchecked.
choices.explanation: Faces do not describe an account change.

choices.text: The exact new recipient and the action requested.
choices.consequence: You have pinned down the change that needs verifying.
choices.explanation: A vague “the CFO approved it” is too thin to check a beneficiary against.

steps.prompt: A fresh start: the invitation includes a callback number for the supplier. Which number do you use?

choices.text: Call the number already in the vendor records.
choices.consequence: The call steps outside the space the invitation controls.
choices.explanation: A number that arrives with the change may belong to the attacker.

choices.text: Call the number in the invitation.
choices.consequence: A cooperative voice confirms the same false instruction.
choices.explanation: That is a second call, but not an independent source.

steps.prompt: A fresh start: you call the supplier on the number in the vendor records and nobody answers. The meeting is demanding approval now. What do you do?

choices.text: Hold the beneficiary change and take it through the escalation and sign-off route.
choices.consequence: The deadline passes, and no unverified transfer goes out.
choices.explanation: No answer is not consent, and confidentiality does not suspend controls.

choices.text: Approve it: a group call counts as two witnesses.
choices.consequence: In this exercise the funds go to the wrong recipient.
choices.explanation: Everyone inside one meeting may come from the same compromised source.

blocks.debrief: The Hong Kong case shows why video cannot be the payment control. This invented exercise adds the two things that do the work: a vendor check through records that predate the request, and a separate approval. Replay any step and compare where the money ends up.

questions.prompt: Does a live-looking group call prove that a payment change is authorised?

choices.text: No; verify the beneficiary and the authority through separate records.
choices.explanation: How a video looks and who may authorise a payment are different questions.
Several faces can all be fed through one controlled call.

questions.prompt: The vendor’s camera glitches during a routine call about an unchanged invoice. What follows?

choices.explanation: Compression artefacts are no reliable verdict.

choices.text: Carry on with the normal checks, and reconnect if needed.
choices.explanation: A glitch can be harmless, and it settles neither identity nor fraud.

questions.prompt: A transfer has gone to a suspected impostor account. What is the first practical step?

choices.text: Wait for the meeting organiser to explain.
choices.explanation: Delay can cut the chance of getting anything back.

choices.text: Contact the sending bank at once about a recall.
choices.explanation: Speed matters, though nothing guarantees recovery.
